justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift assumption from what was likely a base price around $500 for the underlying asset. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price with only a small expected move, reflecting the tendency of prices to exhibit mean-reversion over very short periods and the absence of any imminent catalysts strong enough to shift the estimate materially. At the one-week horizon, I allowed for slightly more drift, recognizing that momentum or gradual trend continuation could push prices modestly higher. By the one-month horizon, the point estimate drifts a bit further upward, consistent with a mild bullish prior that many broad market assets have exhibited over medium-term windows, while still remaining close enough to the base level to reflect genuine uncertainty about direction.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility at each time horizon. For a single day, price moves in liquid assets tend to follow a relatively tight distribution, so a range of roughly plus or minus nine points seemed appropriate. As the horizon extends to one week, the uncertainty compounds, widening the interval to roughly plus or minus eighteen points. By one month, the interval expands further to reflect the accumulating variance over approximately twenty trading days, landing at roughly plus or minus thirty-five points. These widths were informed by the square-root-of-time scaling of volatility, adjusted slightly for the possibility of fat tails in short-term price distributions.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside these stated ranges. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data, an unexpected central bank policy shift toward more aggressive tightening, or a geopolitical shock could easily breach the lower bound of even the one-month interval. On the upside, a surprisingly strong earnings season, a dovish policy pivot, or a sharp short-covering rally could push prices above the upper confidence bound. Liquidity events, such as a flash crash or a broad deleveraging episode, represent tail risks that my intervals do not fully capture, since these tend to produce moves far larger than normal volatility models would suggest.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals implicitly assume a relatively stable volatility regime throughout the forecast period. If volatility itself were to spike, as it does during periods of market stress, the actual distribution of outcomes would be considerably wider and more skewed than what I have described. Conversely, if the market entered an unusually quiet period, realized outcomes might cluster far more tightly than my intervals suggest. The intervals are therefore best understood as reflecting a base-case volatility environment rather than a guarantee of covering all plausible scenarios.
